cards.front: List the 5 layers of the epidermis, deep to superficial.
cards.back: Stratum basale → spinosum → granulosum → lucidum → corneum.

cards.front: What type of epithelium makes up the epidermis?
cards.back: Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium — layered flat cells whose surface cells are filled with keratin.

cards.front: Name the 4 cell types of the epidermis and what each does.
cards.back: Keratinocytes (produce keratin — about 90% of epidermal cells) • Melanocytes (produce the pigment melanin) • Langerhans / dendritic cells (immune defense) • Merkel / tactile cells (touch sensation).

cards.front: What are desmosomes and why do they matter in skin?
cards.back: Strong junctions that bind neighboring keratinocytes together; they resist stretching and shearing so the skin doesn't tear apart.

cards.front: Name the 2 layers of the dermis and the tissue each is made of.
cards.back: Papillary layer — areolar (loose) connective tissue. Reticular layer — dense irregular connective tissue.

cards.front: Name 4 cell types found in the dermis and their functions.
cards.back: Fibroblasts (make collagen and elastin fibers) • Macrophages (engulf debris and pathogens) • Mast cells (release histamine during inflammation) • Adipocytes (fat storage and insulation).

cards.front: What are dermal papillae and what do they do?
cards.back: Fingerlike projections of the papillary dermis reaching up into the epidermis. They form fingerprints, anchor the two layers together, and increase surface area for nutrient exchange.

cards.front: What is keratin — where is it found and what does it do?
cards.back: A tough, waterproof fibrous protein. Found in the outer epidermis, hair, and nails. Protects against abrasion, water loss, and microbes.

cards.front: What are lines of cleavage, and why do surgeons care about them?
cards.back: Tension lines (Langer's lines) following the predominant direction of collagen fibers in the reticular dermis. Incisions made parallel to them gape less and scar less; cuts across them scar more.

cards.front: Name the 2 main types of skin glands — what does each secrete and how?
cards.back: Sebaceous (oil) glands — secrete sebum by holocrine secretion (the whole cell ruptures), usually emptying into hair follicles. Sweat (sudoriferous) glands — secrete sweat by merocrine secretion (exocytosis).

cards.front: What are the 2 types of sweat glands and how do they differ?
cards.back: Eccrine — widespread over the body; watery sweat for cooling (thermoregulation). Apocrine — armpits and groin; thicker, milky secretion activated at puberty; associated with body odor.

cards.front: Name the parts of a hair and the overall functions of hair.
cards.back: Parts: shaft (above the skin), root (below), follicle, bulb, papilla, arrector pili muscle, sebaceous gland. Functions: protection (scalp, nostrils, eyelashes), sensory touch, and heat retention.

cards.front: What does the arrector pili muscle do?
cards.back: A tiny smooth muscle attached to each hair follicle. When it contracts it pulls the hair upright — goosebumps — trapping a layer of air for insulation.

cards.front: Name the parts of a nail — which are visible and which are hidden?
cards.back: Visible: nail plate (body), free edge, lunula (pale half-moon), cuticle (eponychium). Hidden: nail matrix (the growth zone under the base), nail bed, nail fold.

cards.front: What are the functions of nails?
cards.back: Protect the fingertips and toes, improve grip and fine manipulation, and aid scratching.

cards.front: What is the ABCDE rule for spotting a mole that could be cancerous (melanoma)?
cards.back: A — Asymmetry (the two halves don't match) • B — Border irregular or blurred • C — Color varied or multiple colors • D — Diameter over ~6 mm (about a pencil eraser) • E — Evolving (changing size, shape, or color).

cards.front: Describe a first-degree burn.
cards.back: Epidermis only. Red, painful, no blisters — like a mild sunburn. Heals in days without scarring.

cards.front: Describe a second-degree burn.
cards.back: Epidermis plus part of the dermis. Red, very painful, blisters form. Heals in weeks and may scar.

cards.front: Describe a third-degree (full-thickness) burn.
cards.back: Destroys the epidermis and the full dermis. Skin looks white, charred, or leathery; surprisingly little pain at first because nerve endings are destroyed. Requires skin grafting.

cards.front: What is the rule of nines and what is it used for?
cards.back: A method to estimate the percentage of body surface burned in adults: head 9%, each arm 9%, each leg 18%, front torso 18%, back torso 18%, groin 1%. Used to assess severity and guide fluid replacement.
